summary: Georgia's 110-foot Kathleen fire tower, built around 1950, is now the Oaky Woods tower: unmanned since the 1980s and used for radio equipment.

facts.design: Tower with a seven-foot-square watch platform at the top

access.note: On state wildlife management area land. Not open to the general public to climb at will.

visit.trail_note: Supervised visits were suggested by the advocate; the sources describe no arrangement for them.

events.note: Built circa 1950 to provide fire protection in central Georgia.
Aerial watchers took over around 1980. The tower has been unmanned since.
State department bought the land; the tower was renamed the Oaky Woods Fire Tower.

evidence.supports: Built circa 1950 for fire protection around Oaky Woods and Ocmulgee WMAs; 110-foot tower
evidence.quote: Originally known as the Kathleen Fire Tower, this 110-foot tower was built circa 1950 to provide fire protection to the vast woodlands in central Georgia around the Oaky Woods and Ocmulgee Wildlife Management Areas.

evidence.supports: Watch platform is seven feet square
evidence.quote: The windows of the 7-foot-square watch platform were broken out years ago by vandals.

evidence.supports: Forest rangers stood watch in the top of the tower
evidence.quote: when forest rangers stood watch for fires in the top of the tower.

evidence.supports: Aircraft took over lookout duty around 1980; most towers sat empty
evidence.quote: Around 1980 that duty started to be taken over by watchers in aircraft, and most of the towers have sat empty.

evidence.supports: Unmanned since the 1980s; houses radio equipment for local government
evidence.quote: The tower has been unmanned since the 1980s but houses radio equipment for local government.

evidence.supports: State DNR bought the land in 2010 and the tower was renamed Oaky Woods Fire Tower
evidence.quote: The tower sits on land purchased by the Georgia Department of Natural Resources in 2010, at which time the tower was renamed as the Oaky Woods Fire Tower

evidence.supports: Old chair base and fire extinguisher remain in the tower
evidence.quote: The iron base of an old chair where the lookout would have sat is still in the Oaky Woods tower, along with an old fire extinguisher.

evidence.supports: Advocate John Trussell led the effort to save Oaky Woods from development
evidence.quote: Just more than a decade ago Trussell led a successful effort to save Oaky Woods from development
Trussell is trying to get the state, county or private donors to put up about $5,000 it would take to fix up the tower.
That would include replacing the windows, rebuilding the watch platform and replacing the wooden stairs.

evidence.supports: Registered on the National Historic Lookout Register July 30, 2018
Not open to the general public to climb at will; supervised visits suggested
evidence.quote: Although the tower would never be open for the general public to climb at will, Trussell said it could be open for supervised visits.

evidence.supports: Tower sits in the Oaky Woods Wildlife Management Area

sources.title: Macon Telegraph article on the Oaky Woods fire tower, reprinted by Save Oaky Woods

notes_for_editor: Two sources only. The register is the main source for the build and status; the access and condition details come from a reprinted Macon Telegraph column whose original date is unclear on the page. The macon.com original timed out twice and was not used. Current (2026) access is not documented in the sources read, so the access note may be out of date. The record's access field 'unknown' can now read restricted. The register says circa 1950 and the column says built in the 1950s; these agree and are not treated as a conflict.
